paras: The Fort Riley maneuvers clash between Texas militia and Black cavalrymen was a series of confrontations in October 1903 at the army maneuvers camp at Fort Riley, Kansas, after members of a Texas National Guard regiment forbade Black troopers of the Tenth United States Cavalry to pass through their camp. Fist fights followed, and the troopers retaliated against the Texans, though a returning Texas company later denied that any clash took place. Wire reports carried the story nationally, and Black weeklies in Kansas and Iowa printed fuller accounts celebrating the Black soldiers.

Regular troops and National Guard regiments from several states gathered at Fort Riley in October 1903 for joint maneuvers. The Texas provisional regiment's camp lay on the route that troopers of the Tenth Cavalry, described in the wire as "colored men," took to headquarters and to town.

According to a Fort Riley dispatch of October 22, some of the Texas men had forbidden the troopers to pass through their camp "on any pretext," and the troopers were displeased at the order. A special to the Beatrice Daily Express added that an individual Texan tried to enforce the order against a Black cavalryman, but its text breaks off at that point. The dispatch reported numerous fist fights, and a second wire version described "almost a riot" and "scores of fist fights" on the night of October 21. That night, by the wire account, a detachment of troopers raided the Texas camp and carried off one man, who was soon released.

The Topeka Plaindealer gave a different sequence, saying the Texans began taunting the Tenth after the cavalry captured them in a maneuver and said they would have brought bullets had they known they would face "niggers." In its telling, the troopers the next night caught ten or fifteen Texans, whipped them, and tied one up and held him all night until he promised to behave.

A month later the Iowa State Bystander printed the account of an Iowa soldier, who said a Texan knocked down a 17-year-old white servant of an Iowa company for talking with a Black soldier. The Black soldier then struck the Texan on the head with his gun, sending him to the hospital, after which the Texans threatened to "clean up the Negroes" and bar them from their camp. The Iowa men sided with the Black soldiers, who beat several Texans in their camp, after which the Texans were courteous.

The Plaindealer wrote that the commanding officers kept the Texans out of the final exercise and that they left first, "loaded in box cars" for the trip home. No report of arrests, courts-martial or an official inquiry appears in the coverage.

White papers from New Mexico to Maine and Georgia ran the wire on October 22 and 23, often inside a routine maneuvers report, under headlines such as "Texans Dislike Negro Troopers" and "Negro Troopers Row With Texas Soldiers." The wire called the Tenth "one of the best cavalry regiments in the army," while the Wyoming Tribune headlined the raid "Cavalry Abducts Scout." Northern editorial paragraphs in the Minneapolis Journal and the Wichita Daily Eagle mocked the Texans for "drawing the color line too much" and for refusing to drill beside a Black regiment.
In Texas, the San Antonio Daily Light reported that the city's Guard Zouaves had enjoyed a pleasant trip and denied "the report that the Texas troops had a clash with the negro troops."

The Black press treated the episode as a vindication of Black soldiers, with the Topeka Plaindealer's front page headlined "As Usual Texas Got Bad" and calling the Texans "tin soldiers," "bullies" and "disreputable Texas national guards." The Wichita Searchlight noted only "race trouble at Fort Riley" in a news-in-brief column, while the Iowa State Bystander charged that reporters had tried to suppress the incident and called it "a dear lesson" for the Texans.

The accounts differ on the regiment, with the wire, the Beatrice special and the Plaindealer naming the Tenth Cavalry and the Bystander's secondhand report naming the Ninth. They also differ on the scale of the troopers' retaliation, and the San Antonio company denied that any clash occurred.

reader.title: Fort Riley maneuvers clash between Texas militia and Black cavalrymen
bases: Members of a Texas militia regiment forbade Black Tenth Cavalry troopers to pass their camp and taunted and threatened them, leading to fist fights and retaliation by the troopers (A3, A15, A18).

Two separate wire versions, two newspaper specials and two Black-press accounts agree on friction and fights between the Texas regiment and Black cavalrymen (A1, A2, A3, A8, A15, A18), but the returning San Antonio company denied any clash (A17).

framing.detail: The wire called it 'friction,' noted the Tenth was 'one of the best cavalry regiments in the army,' and headline writers chose 'Texans Dislike Negro Troopers,' 'Dislike Negroes' and 'Cavalry Abducts Scout.'
Northern editorial paragraphs mocked the Texans' color line ('drawing the color line too much').
The San Antonio Daily Light printed the home company's denial of any clash.
The Plaindealer headlined 'As Usual Texas Got Bad,' called the Texans 'tin soldiers' and 'bullies,' and celebrated the Tenth's retaliation.
The Bystander said reporters had tried to suppress the incident and called it 'a dear lesson' for the Texans.
